# Cathra: full text

> The full text of every page on cathra.dev, for AI assistants and search tools. Cathra is a free research and education tool that uses machine learning to compare an ovarian ultrasound image to normal and abnormal ovarian appearance, privately in the browser. It is not a medical device and does not diagnose any condition.


---

## Cathra: homepage

Source: https://www.cathra.dev/

Ovarian ultrasound pattern tool

### Cathra compares an ovarian ultrasound to learned patterns.

Choose an existing ultrasound image. Cathra scores how closely it matches a normal and an abnormal ovarian pattern, privately, in your browser.

[How it works →](https://www.cathra.dev/how-it-works)

- Runs on your device
- Nothing is uploaded
- Not a diagnosis

### Why I built Cathra

Cancer has affected me personally. When I looked for tools like this, I found that work in this area is very limited, and there wasn’t a private, free option anyone could explore. I saw that gap and built Cathra to fill it. I’m grateful for all the support, and hearing from people who’ve found it helpful means more to me than I can say. Thank you.

Teddy Aaron, founder · [About Teddy →](https://www.cathra.dev/founder)

**### What is Cathra?**

Cathra is a free research and education tool that uses machine learning to compare an ovarian ultrasound image to two learned patterns: normal ovarian appearance and abnormal ovarian appearance. It runs entirely in your web browser.

#### How it works

A neural network trained on thousands of labeled ovarian ultrasound images from the public PCOSGen dataset scores how closely your image matches each pattern. Most abnormal training images show a polycystic ovarian appearance. [How Cathra works](https://www.cathra.dev/how-it-works)

#### Answers only when confident

A calibrated rule decides when the scores are clear enough to name a pattern. Otherwise Cathra says it can’t tell instead of guessing. [Reading the results](https://www.cathra.dev/how-it-works#confidence)

#### Private by design

Your image is analyzed on your own device and is never uploaded, saved, or sent anywhere. There are no accounts and no cookies. [Privacy & terms](https://www.cathra.dev/privacy)

#### Built for learning

For students, teachers, and researchers exploring how AI reads medical images, with a published paper, a classroom lesson, and a free [dataset check tool](https://www.cathra.dev/dataset-check). It is not a diagnosis. [Cathra research](https://www.cathra.dev/research)

---

## How Cathra works

Source: https://www.cathra.dev/how-it-works

Model card

### How Cathra works

What Cathra was trained on, what its scores mean, and where it falls short.

### What it’s for

You give Cathra an existing ovarian ultrasound image. It compares the image to two visual patterns it learned during training, **normal ovarian appearance** and **abnormal ovarian appearance**, and returns a similarity score for each. Neither result confirms or rules out cancer or any other condition.

### Training data

The current model (v2) was trained on 1,734 labeled ovarian ultrasound images, 867 in each category, and tested on a separate set of 1,449 images it never saw during training. Exact duplicate files were removed. Some test images are near-copies of training images, such as frames from the same scan, which can make test results look better than they are.

- **Normal:** ovaries with a typical appearance.

- **Abnormal:** ovaries that differ from a typical appearance. In this dataset, most abnormal images show a polycystic ovarian appearance.

Dataset credit

Training images come from the **PCOSGen** dataset (train and test sets), created for the Auto-PCOS classification challenge by Palak Handa, Anushka Saini, Siddhant Dutta, Harsh Pathak, Nishi Choudhary, Nidhi Goel, and Jasdeep Kaur Dhanao. Published on Zenodo, 2025: [train](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14592001) · [test](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14591782). Used under the [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) license. Images were sorted into Normal and Abnormal using the dataset’s own labels.

### Test results

I tested both versions of the model on the same 1,449 PCOSGen test images (411 normal, 1,038 abnormal), none of which were used in training. Each image was scored by the same model the website uses, counting the higher of its two scores as the answer.

| | v1 (July 2026) | v2 (November 2026) |
|---|---|---|
| Overall accuracy | 74.2% | **85.6%** |
| Balanced accuracy | 57.6% | **81.1%** |
| Normal images matched correctly | 19.2% (79 of 411) | **70.8%** (291 of 411) |
| Abnormal images matched correctly | **96.0%** (996 of 1,038) | 91.4% (949 of 1,038) |

- **What improved:** v2 recognizes normal images far more reliably, rising from 19% to 71%, so its results are much more balanced across both patterns.

- **What changed slightly:** v2 matches 91% of abnormal images, compared with 96% for v1.

- **Balanced accuracy** gives equal weight to normal and abnormal images. I report it because most of the test images are abnormal.

- **Context:** v2 was trained and tested on images from the same dataset. Results on images from other sources may differ.

Full methods and results are in the [Cathra paper (PDF)](https://www.cathra.dev/cathra-paper.pdf). These are research results on a public image dataset. They are not clinical performance figures and do not describe how Cathra would perform on any individual’s scan.

### Reading the results

Each percentage is a **visual similarity score**: how closely the image resembles that pattern. It is not the probability that a person has any condition.

Cathra names a pattern only when it is confident enough. Its answer rule was calibrated with **conformal prediction**, a statistical method that sets thresholds from test data so that errors stay below a chosen rate. I targeted at most about 1 in 10 wrong answers for each pattern.

- **Normal pattern:** the normal score is 60% or higher.
- **Abnormal pattern:** the abnormal score is about 97% or higher.
- **Anything in between:** “Unable to assess confidently.”

The abnormal bar is higher because the model tends to over-call abnormal. On test images held out from calibration, Cathra gave an answer for about 9 in 10 images, and about 90% of those answers matched the dataset’s label. Normal images wrongly labeled abnormal fell from 28% to about 10%.

This guarantee only applies to images similar to the PCOSGen test set. It says nothing about images from other sources, and it does not make the scores a diagnosis.

### Questions

**Is this a diagnosis?**

No. Cathra is a research and education tool. It shows how closely an image matches two visual patterns it learned. It does not diagnose, detect, confirm, or rule out any condition. Only a qualified medical professional can interpret an ultrasound.

**Is my image stored?**

No. Your image is analyzed on your own device and is never uploaded, saved, or sent anywhere. When you choose another image or close the page, it is discarded.

**What images work?**

A single ovarian ultrasound view, saved as a JPG or PNG. Grayscale and Doppler scans both work. Higher-resolution images with fewer on-screen labels work best. Avoid collages, photos of screens, and screenshots of whole web pages. Cathra analyzes the center square of the image, which it outlines before you analyze.

**Does it detect PCOS?**

No. Cathra compares an image to normal and abnormal ovarian appearance. In its training data, most abnormal images show a polycystic appearance, but PCOS is diagnosed by a doctor using several criteria, not a single image.

**Why does it say “Unable to assess confidently”?**

Cathra only names a pattern when its scores clear a calibrated threshold: 60% or higher for normal, and about 97% or higher for abnormal. When the scores fall in between, it says it can’t tell instead of guessing. See [Reading the results](https://www.cathra.dev#confidence).

### Limitations

- Cathra is a research tool and has not been clinically validated. Like any model, it can be wrong (see [test results](https://www.cathra.dev#results)).

- Its training images come from one public research dataset gathered from online sources. Performance on images from other hospitals, machines, or patient groups hasn’t been tested.

- Image quality, cropping, on-screen labels, and annotations can affect the scores.

- It compares two broad patterns. It doesn’t identify specific conditions or assign clinical categories such as O-RADS.

- It’s designed only for ovarian ultrasound images. Other images can still produce scores, but those scores have no meaning.

Research and education only. Not a medical device or a diagnosis. See [Privacy & terms](https://www.cathra.dev/privacy) for the full disclaimer.

## Cathra research and teaching

Source: https://www.cathra.dev/research

Research

### Cathra research & teaching

The Cathra paper, how to cite it, a free dataset tool, a ready-to-use lesson, and what’s changed. Free for learning and research, not for diagnosis.

### Paper

Cathra: An In-Browser Classifier for Normal and Abnormal Ovarian Ultrasound Appearance

Teddy Aaron · Preprint · Zenodo, November 2026 · DOI [10.5281/zenodo.24118082](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24118082)

- **85.6%** accuracy on 1,449 held-out test images
- **81.1%** balanced accuracy across both classes
- **1,734** training images, equal normal and abnormal

**Abstract**

I built Cathra, a free web tool that compares an existing ovarian ultrasound image to two learned patterns, normal and abnormal, and returns a similarity score for each. The model runs entirely in the browser, so images are never uploaded. I trained the current model (v2) on 1,734 images from the public PCOSGen dataset, balanced between the two classes, and tested it on 1,449 separate images. v2 reached 85.6% accuracy and 81.1% balanced accuracy, matching 91.4% of abnormal and 70.8% of normal test images. My first model (v1) reached 74.2% accuracy on the same images but recognized only 19.2% of normal ones. Cathra is for research and education only and is not a diagnostic tool.

[Read the paper](https://www.cathra.dev/cathra-paper.pdf)

Model v2 on the PCOSGen dataset (Handa et al., 2025, CC BY 4.0). Research results, not clinical performance figures. [Cathra’s full test results and limitations](https://www.cathra.dev/how-it-works#results).

### Cite Cathra

Aaron, T. (2026). *Cathra: An In-Browser Classifier for Normal and Abnormal Ovarian Ultrasound Appearance* [Preprint]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24118082

To cite the tool itself: Aaron, T. (2026). *Cathra* (Version 2) [Computer software]. https://www.cathra.dev. If you use the training data, please also cite the [PCOSGen dataset](https://www.cathra.dev/how-it-works#dataset).

### Dataset Check

Many public medical image datasets contain the same image more than once, sometimes with different labels or in both the training and test sets. That can make a model look more accurate than it is. [Cathra Dataset Check](https://www.cathra.dev/dataset-check) is a free tool that finds these copies in any folder of images, privately in your browser.

[Check a dataset](https://www.cathra.dev/dataset-check)

### Teach with Cathra

A 30-minute lesson on what AI can and can’t do with medical images.

- **Learn (5 min).** Read [how Cathra works](https://www.cathra.dev/how-it-works) together.
- **Try (15 min).** Analyze a few images and note the scores and any “Unable to assess” results.

- **Discuss (10 min).** Pick two questions below.

**Where to find images:** use public, de-identified research datasets, such as PCOS ultrasound datasets on [Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/search?q=pcos+ultrasound) or [PCOSGen](https://www.cathra.dev/how-it-works#dataset). Check each dataset’s license before using it. Don’t use personal or patient scans.

**Discussion questions**

- Why is a similarity score not the same as a diagnosis?
- Version 1 scored 74% overall but got only 19% of normal images right. How can one number be misleading?

- Why might results differ on scans from another hospital?
- Who is responsible when a medical AI tool is wrong?

Using Cathra with a class or lab? Email [paultaaron@icloud.com](mailto:paultaaron@icloud.com?subject=Cathra%20for%20my%20institution) with your organization’s name and how you plan to use it.

## Cathra Dataset Check

Source: https://www.cathra.dev/dataset-check

Free tool

### Cathra Dataset Check

Find copied and mislabeled images in a medical image dataset before you train or test a model. It runs in your browser, and nothing is uploaded.

Drop a dataset folder here Folder names become labels, for example Normal/ and Abnormal/. Add train/ and test/ folders to check for leaks.

How similar counts as a near-copy: Very close (recommended)

Your images stay on this device. Cathra never sees them, their names, or the results.

### Why this matters

If the same scan appears in both the training and test sets, a model can look more accurate than it really is. If the same scan is labeled two different ways, no model can get both right. While building Cathra, I found both problems in a public ovarian ultrasound dataset, so I made this check free for anyone.

### How it works

Each image is shrunk to a tiny grayscale “fingerprint” (a perceptual hash). Images whose fingerprints are almost the same look almost the same, even if they were resized, re-saved, or slightly cropped. Exact copies are confirmed with a file checksum.

Similar-looking images aren’t always true copies. Review the matches before removing anything. Research use only.

## Cathra privacy and terms

Source: https://www.cathra.dev/privacy

Privacy policy and terms

### Cathra privacy & terms

Effective November 11, 2026. Cathra is operated by Teddy Aaron Ventures LLC. The short version: your image never leaves your device.

### Your images

When you choose an image, your browser loads it into memory and the model analyzes it on your device. The image is **never uploaded, sent to a server, saved, logged, or stored** by Cathra. When you choose another image or close the page, it is discarded.

### What we collect

Cathra has no accounts, no sign-up, and no forms. We do not collect your name, email, health information, or the results of any analysis. Cathra does not use advertising or cookies, and it does not track you across sites.

If you email us, we receive your email address and whatever you choose to include. We use it only to reply, and we never sell or share it.

### Visit counts

We use Vercel Web Analytics to count page visits, such as how many people opened the tool. It uses no cookies, does not identify you, and does not follow you across sites. It never sees your image or your results.

### Hosting and libraries

Like any website, the services that deliver Cathra’s files receive standard technical information when your browser requests them, such as your IP address, browser type, and the time of the request. These are:

- **Vercel**, which hosts the website and the model files.

- **jsDelivr**, a public CDN that delivers the TensorFlow.js and Teachable Machine libraries.

These requests are only for Cathra’s own code and model. Your image is never part of them. Each provider handles this information under its own privacy policy.

### Medical & legal disclaimer

Cathra is a research and educational demonstration only. It is not a medical device, is not FDA-cleared or approved, and does not diagnose, treat, cure, prevent, detect, confirm, or rule out ovarian cancer or any other medical condition. Using it does not create a doctor-patient relationship. Results are computer-generated similarity scores provided “as is,” without warranties of any kind, and may be inaccurate or incomplete. Do not use them to make, delay, or disregard any medical decision, and always consult a qualified, licensed medical professional. You use Cathra entirely at your own risk.

### Ownership

Cathra is owned and operated by Teddy Aaron Ventures LLC. Cathra’s model, code, and design are proprietary and protected by copyright. You may not copy, download, redistribute, modify, or reverse-engineer them without written permission.

### Other

Cathra is not directed to children under 13. If this page changes, we will update it here and change the effective date above. Questions about privacy, terms, or permissions: [paultaaron@icloud.com](mailto:paultaaron@icloud.com?subject=Cathra)

## What does a normal ovary look like on ultrasound?

Source: https://www.cathra.dev/learn/normal-ovary-ultrasound

[Learn](https://www.cathra.dev/learn)

### What does a normal ovary look like on ultrasound?

A short, plain-English guide to reading a normal ovary on an ultrasound image.

From Cathra · Updated November 25, 2026 · General education, not medical advice

Short answer

On ultrasound, a normal ovary in an adult of reproductive age usually looks like a small, oval, mid-gray structure with a few small, dark, round spots. Those spots are follicles, tiny fluid-filled sacs that hold developing eggs. Their number and size change throughout the menstrual cycle.

### Reading the gray, black, and white

Ultrasound images are built from sound echoes, so they show structures in shades of gray:

- **Black:** fluid, such as the inside of a follicle or a cyst. Fluid lets sound pass through without echoing.
- **Gray:** soft tissue, such as the ovary’s inner tissue (the stroma).
- **Bright white:** denser surfaces that reflect a lot of sound.

### What a typical ovary shows

- **Shape and size:** an oval structure, usually a few centimeters long. An ovarian volume of 10 mL or more is one of the signs doctors look for when considering polycystic ovarian morphology.
- **Small follicles:** several small, dark, round follicles, usually spread through the ovary.
- **One larger follicle mid-cycle:** as ovulation approaches, one follicle usually grows larger than the rest before it releases an egg.
- **After ovulation:** the follicle that released the egg becomes the corpus luteum, which can look like a small, thick-walled structure.

### What changes the picture

- **Cycle timing:** the same ovary can look quite different at the start, middle, and end of a cycle.
- **Age:** after menopause, ovaries are usually smaller and show few or no follicles. Before puberty they are also small.
- **Hormonal birth control** can reduce follicle growth.
- **Simple, fluid-filled cysts** are common and often part of the normal cycle. A doctor decides whether any follow-up is needed.

### How the scan is done

Ovaries are usually imaged with a **transvaginal** ultrasound, which gives the clearest view, or a **transabdominal** ultrasound through the lower belly. The exam is painless or mildly uncomfortable and uses no radiation.

### How Cathra relates to this

Cathra learned a “normal ovarian appearance” pattern from ultrasound images labeled normal in the public PCOSGen dataset. It compares a new image to that pattern and gives a similarity score. It cannot tell you whether an ovary is healthy; only a qualified professional reading the full exam can do that.

**Try Cathra.** Compare an ovarian ultrasound image to learned patterns, free and privately in your browser.

[Open the tool](https://www.cathra.dev/analyze)

### Sources

- MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine). Transvaginal ultrasound. [medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003779.htm](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003779.htm)
- Teede HJ, Tay CT, Laven JJE, et al. Recommendations from the 2023 international evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2023;108(10):2447–2469. [doi.org/10.1210/clinem/dgad463](https://doi.org/10.1210/clinem/dgad463)
- Handa P, Saini A, Dutta S, et al. PCOSGen-train and PCOSGen-test datasets. Zenodo; 2025. CC BY 4.0. [doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14592001](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14592001)

## What does a polycystic ovary look like on ultrasound?

Source: https://www.cathra.dev/learn/polycystic-ovary-ultrasound

[Learn](https://www.cathra.dev/learn)

### What does a polycystic ovary look like on ultrasound?

What “polycystic ovarian morphology” means, how it is measured, and how it relates to PCOS.

From Cathra · Updated November 25, 2026 · General education, not medical advice

Short answer

A polycystic ovary usually looks larger than average and contains many small, dark, round follicles, often arranged around its outer edge. Under the 2023 international PCOS guideline, doctors call this polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM) in adults when one ovary has 20 or more follicles, or an ovarian volume of 10 mL or more.

### What doctors look for

- **Many small follicles:** numerous small, dark, fluid-filled follicles in one or both ovaries, often lined up around the edge.
- **Follicle count:** 20 or more follicles in at least one ovary, counted on a transvaginal scan with a modern, high-frequency probe.
- **Ovarian volume:** 10 mL or more in at least one ovary. Volume is used on its own when image quality or older equipment makes counting follicles unreliable.
- These measurements are taken when there is no dominant follicle, corpus luteum, or cyst that would change them.

### Polycystic ovaries are not the same as PCOS

The name is confusing. **Polycystic ovarian morphology** describes how an ovary looks. **Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)** is a hormonal condition. In adults, PCOS is diagnosed when at least two of these three are present, after other causes have been ruled out:

- irregular periods or ovulation problems,
- signs of high androgens (“male” hormones), seen in symptoms or blood tests,
- polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound, or a high AMH blood level.

That means someone can have polycystic-looking ovaries without PCOS, and someone can have PCOS with normal-looking ovaries.

### Teens are different

Many teenagers naturally have ovaries with lots of follicles. The guideline says ultrasound should not be used to diagnose PCOS in adolescents, generally within 8 years of their first period.

### How Cathra relates to this

In the PCOSGen dataset Cathra learned from, most images labeled abnormal show a polycystic ovarian appearance. Cathra compares a new image to that learned pattern. It does not count follicles, measure volume, or diagnose PCOS, and its scores should never be used to make a medical decision.

**Try Cathra.** Compare an ovarian ultrasound image to learned patterns, free and privately in your browser.

[Open the tool](https://www.cathra.dev/analyze)

### Sources

- Teede HJ, Tay CT, Laven JJE, et al. Recommendations from the 2023 international evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2023;108(10):2447–2469. [doi.org/10.1210/clinem/dgad463](https://doi.org/10.1210/clinem/dgad463)
- MedlinePlus Genetics. Polycystic ovary syndrome. [medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/polycystic-ovary-syndrome/](https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/polycystic-ovary-syndrome/)
- Handa P, Saini A, Dutta S, et al. PCOSGen-train and PCOSGen-test datasets. Zenodo; 2025. CC BY 4.0. [doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14592001](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14592001)

## How accurate is AI at reading ultrasounds?

Source: https://www.cathra.dev/learn/ai-ultrasound-accuracy

[Learn](https://www.cathra.dev/learn)

### How accurate is AI at reading ultrasounds?

What accuracy numbers really mean, using Cathra’s own test results as a worked example.

From Cathra · Updated November 25, 2026 · General education, not medical advice

Short answer

It depends on the tool, the task, and especially how it was tested. A single accuracy number can look impressive while hiding serious weaknesses, so it helps to know a few other measures and to ask where the test images came from.

### Why one number can mislead

Cathra’s first model (v1) scored **74.2% accuracy** on 1,449 test images. That sounds decent, but it correctly recognized only **19.2% of normal images**. Because most test images were abnormal, a model that called almost everything abnormal still looked fairly accurate.

Cathra’s current model (v2) was trained on balanced data. It scored 85.6% accuracy and, more importantly, recognized 70.8% of normal images and 91.4% of abnormal ones.

### The measures that matter

- **Sensitivity:** of the truly abnormal images, how many the AI called abnormal.
- **Specificity:** of the truly normal images, how many the AI called normal.
- **Balanced accuracy:** the average of the two, so a lopsided test set can’t hide a weak spot. Cathra v1 scored 57.6% here; v2 scored 81.1%.
- **Positive predictive value:** when the AI says “abnormal,” how often it is right. This depends heavily on how common the condition is in the group being tested.

### Where the test images came from matters most

- **Same source vs. new sources:** models are often tested on images from the same dataset they learned from. Results on images from other hospitals, machines, or patients are usually lower.
- **Near-duplicate images:** if test images are near-copies of training images, results look better than they really are. [Learn why](https://www.cathra.dev/learn/duplicate-images-medical-ai).
- **Confidence:** a good tool should say when it isn’t sure. Cathra only names a pattern when its scores clear calibrated thresholds, and otherwise says it can’t tell.

### Questions to ask about any ultrasound AI

- What were sensitivity and specificity, not just accuracy?
- Was it tested on images from different hospitals or machines?
- Were duplicate or near-duplicate images removed before testing?
- Has it been reviewed or cleared by a regulator for clinical use?

Cathra is a research and education tool. It has not been clinically validated or cleared by any regulator, and its results come from one public dataset.

**Try Cathra.** Compare an ovarian ultrasound image to learned patterns, free and privately in your browser.

[Open the tool](https://www.cathra.dev/analyze)

- Collins GS, Moons KGM, Dhiman P, et al. TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction models that use regression or machine learning methods. BMJ. 2024;385:e078378. [doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2023-078378](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2023-078378)
- Handa P, Saini A, Dutta S, et al. PCOSGen-train and PCOSGen-test datasets. Zenodo; 2025. CC BY 4.0. [doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14592001](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14592001)

## Can AI detect PCOS from an ultrasound?

Source: https://www.cathra.dev/learn/can-ai-detect-pcos

[Learn](https://www.cathra.dev/learn)

### Can AI detect PCOS from an ultrasound?

An honest look at what ultrasound AI can and cannot tell you about PCOS.

From Cathra · Updated November 25, 2026 · General education, not medical advice

Short answer

No. An AI tool cannot diagnose PCOS from an ultrasound alone. PCOS is diagnosed by a clinician using symptoms, blood tests, and ruling out other conditions. At most, ultrasound AI can estimate whether an image resembles a polycystic ovarian appearance, which is only one part of one diagnostic criterion.

### Why an ultrasound alone isn’t enough

In adults, PCOS is diagnosed when at least two of three features are present: irregular periods or ovulation problems, signs of high androgens, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound (or a high AMH blood level). Other conditions must be ruled out first. An image can only speak to one of those three, and many people with polycystic-looking ovaries don’t have PCOS.

### What ultrasound AI can do in research

- Compare an image to patterns learned from labeled examples.
- Help researchers and students study how image AI behaves, including its mistakes.
- Highlight how dataset quality, such as duplicate or mislabeled images, affects results.

### What it can’t do

- Diagnose PCOS or any other condition.
- Account for symptoms, hormone levels, age, or cycle timing.
- Replace an ultrasound exam read by a qualified professional.

### Be careful with PCOS AI claims

If an app says it can “detect” or “diagnose” PCOS from a photo or scan, ask how it was tested, on whose images, and whether it has been cleared for medical use. Treat high accuracy claims with caution unless they are backed by testing on images from many different sources.

### Where Cathra fits

Cathra compares an ovarian ultrasound to normal and abnormal appearance patterns. Most abnormal images it learned from show a polycystic appearance, but Cathra does not detect or diagnose PCOS. It is a free research and education tool, and it runs privately in your browser.

### Quick answers

**Can AI diagnose PCOS?**

No. PCOS is diagnosed by a clinician using symptoms, blood tests, and ultrasound or AMH, after ruling out other causes. AI cannot make that diagnosis from an image.

**Does Cathra detect PCOS?**

No. Cathra compares an ovarian ultrasound to normal and abnormal appearance patterns for research and education. It does not detect or diagnose PCOS or any other condition.

**Do polycystic ovaries mean PCOS?**

Not necessarily. Polycystic-looking ovaries are common, especially in teenagers, and are only one of three criteria used to diagnose PCOS in adults.

## Why duplicate images make medical AI look better than it is

Source: https://www.cathra.dev/learn/duplicate-images-medical-ai

[Learn](https://www.cathra.dev/learn)

### Why duplicate images make medical AI look better than it is

How copied and mislabeled images quietly inflate results, and how to check a dataset for free.

From Cathra · Updated November 25, 2026 · General education, not medical advice

Short answer

When the same or nearly the same image appears in both the training set and the test set, an AI model is partly being tested on images it has already seen. That makes its accuracy look higher than it would be on truly new images. When the same image appears with two different labels, no model can get both right.

### How duplicates sneak in

- **Video frames:** ultrasound datasets often include several frames from the same scan, which look almost identical.
- **Re-saved or resized copies:** the same picture saved at a different size or quality.
- **Images collected from the web:** the same image can be downloaded from several places.

### A real example

Running [Cathra Dataset Check](https://www.cathra.dev/dataset-check) on the public PCOSGen ovarian ultrasound dataset (4,569 images after removing exact duplicate files), at its recommended setting, flagged:

- **3,626 images (79%)** that have at least one near-copy in the dataset,
- **5,173 near-copy pairs** that cross the training and test sets, and
- **7,939 near-copy pairs** where the two images carry different labels.

Looking similar isn’t always the same as being a true copy, so matches should be reviewed by hand. Still, numbers like these mean test results on this dataset, including Cathra’s own, may look better than they would on images from new sources. Cathra says so on its [How it works](https://www.cathra.dev/how-it-works) page.

### How to avoid it

- Remove exact and near-duplicate images before splitting data into training and test sets.
- Split by patient or by scan, not by individual image, so frames from one scan stay together.
- Review images that appear with conflicting labels.
- Report results on a cleaned test set, and say what was removed.

### Check a dataset for free

[Cathra Dataset Check](https://www.cathra.dev/dataset-check) finds exact copies, near-copies, conflicting labels, and train/test leaks in a folder of images. It runs entirely in your browser, so nothing is uploaded.

**Try Cathra.** Compare an ovarian ultrasound image to learned patterns, free and privately in your browser.

[Open the tool](https://www.cathra.dev/analyze)
